Editorial: The Philippines must feel pain before the forces behind it grow dispirited

What exactly is happening in the waters around Huangyan Island (Scarborough Shoal)? What is implied by the standoff between Chinese maritime law enforcement and fishing vessels and Philippine ships? The real answer to this question will determine China’s next moves.

China’s opponents over Huangyan Island are complicated. Besides the Philippines, which claims sovereignty over those reefs, there are the United States and Western forces who want to use this friction to increase Asia’s hostility toward a rising China. Countries such as Vietnam and Japan, which also have maritime territorial disputes with China, are likewise eager to see trouble at Huangyan and to test ‘wolf-pack’ tactics against China.

If the Huangyan dispute is viewed only as a simple China–Philippines power contest, ending the crisis would not require too much thought. But China’s task is much broader than merely defending Huangyan Island. China must also counter external forces that would use this incident to disrupt and undermine China’s fundamental goal of national rise. These complex tasks cannot be accomplished by a quick, decisive clash with the Philippines alone; nevertheless, suppressing Philippine brazenness is the most critical link that currently affects the whole situation.

Both China and the Philippines therefore have an interest in a peaceful resolution because the Philippines knows that if it acts it will suffer a crushing defeat. China also understands that beating the Philippines at sea does not exactly address all of our most urgent problems.

China now is like ten fingers pressing on ten fleas; we must be very clear-headed. We must not, in a fit of anger, forget the other fleas when we strike one. But we must also not lose the flexibility to act and shy away from handling at least one.

The golden period for a once-and-for-all solution to the South China Sea issue has been missed. The hard, prolonged process of solving it is a geopolitical reality Chinese people must face. What we must actually do is increase our active control over this process, not allow other forces to lead us by the nose.

To do this China must show composure, demonstrate resolve in the South China Sea, and exhibit calm in the face of multiple challenges. The current priority is to teach the Philippines a lesson, to make it feel real pain for some time to come. The Philippines’ sense of failure will in part translate into dejection among the forces behind it.

China should have contingency plans to fight a small-scale naval war with the Philippines. Once fighting begins, we must strike forcefully, sending a clear message to the outside world that China “does not want war but is not afraid of war.” At the same time we should be clear that such a war would not be the end of the South China Sea issue; the Chinese people must be prepared for a marathon-style defense of the islands we are not very familiar with. Meanwhile, we do not mind a temporary escalation of conflict. Whether to fight or not depends on a flick of the switch in Manila.

Among the many challenges in the South China Sea, Manila’s arrogance is the most conspicuous; we must prevent its provocation from becoming a platform for coordinated containment of China. China needs to develop various economic and political means to strike the Philippines, so that the losses Manila suffers far exceed its gains, and so that its role is not attractive to any other Asian country.

Geoeconomics and geopolitics in Asia are almost separate. China already occupies the center of Asia’s geoeconomics, but remains passive politically. China should strive to at least partially connect these two systems, and should not allow Asian economic and political interests to diverge without limit.

A full cold-shouldering of the Philippines should become China’s clear policy for the coming period. China must be willing to bear the losses caused to ourselves by sanctioning the Philippines, in exchange for much greater losses inflicted upon the Philippines. Making that decision should be no harder than sending the navy to fight the Philippines.

Defending the South China Sea islands is not empty talk; it requires patience, cost, and perseverance.

Editorial: EU wine in the “double anti” is not China’s only bullet

On the 5th China announced the launch of anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations into European Union wine. This is clearly a response to the European Commission’s announcement on the 4th that it would impose a temporary anti-dumping duty on Chinese photovoltaic (PV) products. This test has only just begun, and how successfully China responds will have long-term significance.

The EU’s announced temporary anti-dumping rate is 11.8%, which is relatively low compared with the 47% it had threatened; this shows that earlier Chinese representations and Premier Li Keqiang’s visit to Europe had some effect, and that the EU is somewhat wary of possible Chinese reprisals.

China has struck at EU wine. Although its trade volume is only about 1/20 of China’s PV exports to Europe, it first hits countries such as France and Italy that supported the EU’s “double anti” investigation into Chinese PV products. Besides, China still has other cards such as buying euro-denominated bonds and investing in Europe; EU electromechanical products, chemical products and others export to China hundreds of billions of dollars every year. China can, depending on Europe’s response, gradually play those cards.

Because Chinese-made solar panels are a part of the European photovoltaic industry for which it is hard to find same-price, same-quality substitutes, if Chinese solar panels are sanctioned many European companies will suffer. That is why more than a dozen EU countries and hundreds of European companies opposed the EU’s “double anti” on Chinese solar panels. China has the conditions to “drive a wedge” inside the EU in this conflict.

Now China needs to act more forcefully, to stimulate debate within the EU and make public opinion exert greater pressure on the European Commission. Even if this cannot roll back the clock on EU trade protectionism, it can at least avoid the worst outcome of a permanent 47% anti-dumping duty on Chinese PV products.

In war, the negotiating basis between belligerents is the situation on the battlefield; the same logic applies to trade wars. Whether the EU will seriously negotiate and compromise with China depends on whether doing so is more beneficial to the EU — on whether the reciprocal sanctions would hurt the EU more than not imposing them.

Whatever the final result, this incident is a wake-up call for China’s PV industry. The low-price strategy has run its course; vicious competition within the industry will hasten the arrival of unforeseen disasters. The Chinese PV industry once rode on the edge of high technology, but some of its chaotic practices are not much different from the clothing and toy industries.

This is also a warning about China’s overall exports. China continues to face anti-dumping investigations, but this time the export value involved reaches more than US$20 billion, a record. Although the EU’s “double anti” has selfish elements, we should recognize that selfishness is the nature of the world market. The EU’s aggressive reaction once again faintly outlines the “boundary” of how much external markets will tolerate the spillover from China’s economic growth.

International trade rules are only upheld when they serve the interests of great powers. Free trade was actively promoted by the US and Europe because it then best served those developed countries’ interests. China adapted to those rules and prospered; now free trade is more beneficial to China than to the US and Europe, so the US and Europe have returned to trade protectionism. They will find reasons to discount existing rules and, if that does not work, they will change the rules or even create alternative trade systems. The US is now negotiating the TPP with Asia-Pacific countries and preparing TTIP with European countries to rebuild arrangements favorable to the US and the West.

If China does not rapidly expand the capacity of its domestic market, it will gradually slip into strategic passivity, and the potential of China’s rise will be exhausted. The world will not allow China to be a monopolistic processing center while other countries separately shoulder the roles of raw-material suppliers and consumer markets. Overall, only with a larger domestic market will China’s ability to win foreign markets grow.

China’s reform and opening-up indeed face an important upgrade, and the necessary adjustments are considerable. We must fight every battle well, and at the same time be clear about strategic direction. The information contained in this China–EU anti-dumping conflict goes far beyond the photovoltaic industry itself. We must both defend our interests and lay groundwork for the future, and also calmly and carefully unpack and understand these signals.

Editorial: On the North Korean nuclear crisis, China need not worry about pleasing anyone

On the 24th North Korea responded more sharply to the Security Council resolution of the previous day, declaring it would carry out a “high-level nuclear test.” This very likely is not just bluster — South Korea says preparations for a new North Korean nuclear test are indeed underway.

The Security Council resolution on the 23rd was adopted in response to North Korea’s recent launch of a “man-made earth satellite,” and it broadened the scope of sanctions on North Korean organizations and individuals. China voted in favor after making major changes to the draft resolution.

But North Korea does not seem grateful. In its 24th statement it criticized China without naming it, saying that “even a great power that should take the lead in building a just world order is suppressed by U.S. arrogance and might, so muddled as to even abandon the minimum principles it must uphold.”

China faces a severe dilemma. Not only is the goal of peninsula denuclearization becoming ever more distant, but seeking a diplomatic balance among North Korea, South Korea, Japan and the United States has become nearly impossible.

Since the situation can hardly get any worse, China should relax and lower its expectations that its strategy will fully succeed on the peninsula. It should deal with the pressing problems realistically, no longer pursuing a single absolute goal but instead seeking the best balance between resources invested and strategic returns.

China should continue to uphold the principle of addressing both symptoms and root causes in the peninsula nuclear issue. Persisting in calling for denuclearization keeps the moral high ground on the peninsula and gives China room to maneuver against extreme positions from any side.

China must not become a party to the peninsula conflict as the U.S. and Japan have done, but it should not imagine it can remain entirely detached and successfully please both sides. If we become involved to some degree and thereby offend one or both sides, we should accept that frankly.

That stance will restore some strategic ease to China: we will not be held hostage by any side’s extreme demands, and can instead set a clearer set of principles for responding to specific conflicts. Much of the energy we spend trying to persuade other parties can instead be devoted to defending our own principle framework.

For example, the current scale of China’s assistance to North Korea reflects China–DPRK friendship and also embodies our attitude toward the current situation on the peninsula. China’s role and stance in Security Council discussions on North Korea are also clear. If North Korea conducts a new nuclear test or again launches a “satellite,” China should without hesitation reduce its aid to North Korea. If South Korea, Japan and the United States push the Security Council to impose extreme sanctions on North Korea, China should resolutely stop them and force them to amend the draft.

North Korea may become “angry” — let it be. We must not refrain from action out of worry that China–DPRK friendship will be harmed. South Korea, Japan and the United States may loudly criticize China — let them. We are under no obligation to appease them, and even if we wanted to we could not.

China’s power is there; if we are resolute the situation will gradually adapt to our principles and positions, slowly reducing the excessive demands from each side that we should accommodate their separate interests.

China is a major power and borders the Korean Peninsula; this determines the complexity and multiplicity of our strategic interests. We cannot in any case take sides between the parties on the peninsula. When disputes are confused and chaotic, China must maximize protection of its own interests rather than those of any other party. If either side on the peninsula cannot understand this, let them come to understand it slowly.

China hopes for peninsula stability, but if a major upheaval really occurs, it is not the end of the world — that should be China’s bottom line. China’s capacity to endure is surely greater than that of North or South Korea and is greater than Japan’s; it may not be lower than the United States’. Therefore China is a promoter of peace on the peninsula and bears great-power responsibility for peace and stability in Northeast Asia, but we are by no means first on anyone’s list of those who fear disorder.

Everyone says “take a step back and the sea widens the sky”; while China cannot withdraw in action, it should be able to take that step back mentally. China is destined to be amid the disorder of East Asia, but fortunately it is the strongest among the regional countries. Whoever causes disorder will first harm themselves; when the water reaches our knees, it will reach their necks. China must calm itself and maintain resolve.

Editorial: Countering THAAD — Five recommended national actions

On the 8th, the United States and South Korea formally announced the deployment of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) antimissile system by U.S. forces stationed in South Korea. The two countries use the rationale that the deployment will protect South Korea from the threats of North Korean nuclear weapons, weapons of mass destruction, and ballistic missiles. South Korea said it will decide the specific site for THAAD within a few weeks and complete the deployment before the end of 2017.

On the 8th, China’s Foreign Ministry quickly stated its firm opposition to the U.S.-ROK deployment of THAAD, urging the two countries not to take actions that would complicate the regional situation or do things that damage China’s strategic security interests.

Russia has long opposed the U.S.-ROK THAAD deployment as well; China and Russia’s leaders recently expressed a consistent position of opposition in some joint statements.

Besides monitoring North Korean missile activity, the THAAD system can expand its surveillance range to China’s Northeast and North China regions, as well as to Russia’s Far East, thereby eroding the strategic security of China and Russia. South Korea has long claimed it can reduce THAAD’s surveillance range, but first, THAAD is controlled by U.S. forces stationed in Korea and Korea does not have the final say; second, such cheap promises are meaningless in international politics.

The U.S. and South Korea chose the 8th to announce their formal decision to deploy THAAD, probably because of the imminent ruling on the South China Sea arbitration and China’s diplomatic attention being drawn to the South China Sea. This is also a kind of “taking advantage of someone’s difficulty.”

However, Northeast Asia — a direction that concerns China’s strategic interests — will not be ignored, and challenges coming from that direction must be answered. North Korea’s nuclear test, which led China to decide on sanctions against the DPRK, and the U.S. and South Korea’s insistence on deploying THAAD — China naturally must make a strong response.

We recommend China take the following targeted measures:

First, sanction the specific South Korean administrative counties that accept THAAD missile deployment; sanction South Korean companies and service organizations connected with the THAAD deployment; China will no longer have economic ties or other exchanges with them, and will no longer accept their products into the Chinese market.

Second, sanction South Korean political figures who actively promote THAAD deployment, restrict their entry into China, and sanction their family businesses.

Third, the People’s Liberation Army should study and develop response plans to minimize the strategic damage THAAD could cause to us; these should at least include technical jamming of THAAD and putting the system under missile targeting in a war-ready posture.

Fourth, re-evaluate the long-term effects of sanctions on North Korea regarding the situation in Northeast Asia, and consider sanctions on North Korea in connection with the imbalance in the region after THAAD deployment.

Fifth, explore the possibility of China and Russia taking joint actions to offset the effects produced by the U.S.-ROK deployment of THAAD.

The U.S.-ROK deployment of THAAD will inevitably produce long-term and significant strategic ripples. From now on South Korea will be tied more tightly to the U.S.-ROK alliance, its diplomatic and strategic independence will diminish, and it may further become “Japanized.” This is completely not what China hopes to see, but we are not powerless. Relying on forbearance to prevent South Korea from further leaning toward the United States will be futile; we can only respond to changes realistically.

The North Korean nuclear issue has made the peninsula situation more complicated, but North Korea’s possession of nuclear weapons also has deep causes beyond Pyongyang’s own control. The greatest root of regional disorder is the United States’ continued maintenance of a Cold War posture on the peninsula, and its increased intention to use the Northeast Asia direction to contain China. Perhaps one cannot simply blame Pyongyang or Seoul; in the end, Northeast Asia is still a dispute between China and the United States.

The Korea Peninsula issue cannot be clearly seen from the perspectives of Pyongyang or Seoul alone. China–North Korea relations have already been affected, and China–South Korea relations are likely to suffer to some extent as well. Compared with the United States, whether China is strong or not, it is currently in a period of "growing pains." We need to accept that at this stage China will not please everyone; neither indulge ourselves nor be overly hard on ourselves. Be a genuine China, and when we look around, no challenge is insurmountable.

Editorial: Australia has become the United States' loudspeaker in the Asia-Pacific

Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has also been gesturing and directing China on its North Korea policy. In an interview broadcast on Australian radio station 2SM on August 31 he said China has the greatest influence over North Korea, "therefore the greatest responsibility." "They could go further, for example by cutting off oil supplies."

In the interview Turnbull called North Korea a "mafia state," and said that if the North Korean leader launched a war, "for him it would be like a death sentence." He stated that if the United States were attacked, Australia would help the United States. Earlier he told U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson that in a wartime situation Australia "would not shirk, and would support the United States without hesitation."

Australia, like the United Kingdom, is far from the Korean Peninsula — separated by roughly a Pacific Ocean. Turnbull suddenly pokes his head over and, so specifically, "pressures" China. His words are more excessive than Theresa May's vague call for China to "do all it can." Although President Trump has complained about China in inconsistent statements, he has so far never publicly asked China to cut off North Korea's oil — who gave the Australian prime minister the presumptuous idea that he could advise China in this way?

We suspect that after being publicly rebuked by Trump earlier this year — and having been too timid to respond — Prime Minister Turnbull is trying to flatter Washington. Australia is often seen as a "second-class Western citizen," and therefore has tried hard to show itself, to demonstrate loyalty to the United States. What Washington says, Canberra repeats and echoes; now even things Washington has not said, Canberra is eager to speak for.

But Washington may not welcome Canberra's performance this time, because Turnbull's words are just words and bring no action. Beijing cannot take such words seriously, nor will it keep them in mind.

China is adjacent to North Korea; when it comes to North Korea developing nuclear weapons and medium- and long-range missiles, China's concern is not comparable to Australia’s. To sanction North Korea, Australia doesn't need to exert effort or bear losses; if the Peninsula erupts into conflict, refugees would not come to Australia. For a country so far away to swagger and, as if on moral high ground, tell China in detail what to do — how can that not be annoying?

Australian media often criticize China; that is their freedom of speech. The Global Times has also criticized Australia, calling it the U.S. global policeman's deputy in the Asia-Pacific — a paper cat following behind America's paper tiger. But for the Australian prime minister to shout at China outside the Security Council is diplomatically rude. How to sanction North Korea is something only the Security Council can decide.

Perhaps we should draw another portrait of Australia: it is a loudspeaker the United States has erected in the Asia-Pacific. The loudspeaker works hard and is proud, but it is increasingly becoming local noise — self-righteously blathering away, imagining itself a genuine and noble guardian.

In recent years Canberra has become one of the most active sources of hawkish voices toward China; it is even more eager than some of the West's "first-class citizens" to stick its neck out on China-related issues. This is like certain zealous Korean missionaries who are keener to stir up trouble in sensitive areas than Western missionaries.

There are also voices among the Chinese public proposing that if North Korea carries out a sixth nuclear test, the Chinese government should cut or reduce oil supplies to North Korea. But whether China plays that card, and how it does so, is China's own affair. China has strictly implemented the Security Council's sanctions resolutions on North Korea. The Australian government has an obligation to maintain a relationship of mutual respect with the Chinese government; the Security Council's whistle will not be hung around Australia's neck, and its loose talk amounts to blowing a foul whistle from the stands.

Australia needs to learn self-respect. Its current political culture appears more radical than its European roots, resulting in a mismatch. Canberra should look in the mirror of international rules and ask itself how it should treat its largest trading partner China. If it truly wants to contribute to a peaceful resolution of the North Korean nuclear issue, it ought to correct its role.

Editorial: Canada’s rough treatment of Meng Wanzhou is a serious violation of human rights

A bail hearing for Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou was held Friday at the British Columbia Supreme Court; the court adjourned without a ruling and will resume on Monday.

According to foreign media citing court reporters, Meng wore a green top in court and was not handcuffed; she appeared to have been treated humanely. But that is only an illusion.

The Global Times, through informed sources, understands that since Meng Wanzhou was detained on December 1 she has been treated roughly and in a way that insults her dignity. When Canadian police arrested her at the airport and took her to the detention center they put handcuffs on her; that night, during the routine trip to the hospital and back to the detention center, she was handcuffed. When she was taken from the detention center to court, and after the hearing when she was taken to the correctional centre, she was not only handcuffed but also shackled.

Putting on restraint devices that are used for serious criminals, and directly treating her as a serious criminal before any trial or conviction, tramples her basic human rights and insults her personhood.

We understand Meng had surgery to remove her thyroid in May and she also has high blood pressure and needs to take medication on time every day. But Canada’s detention facility has not provided the care her current health requires.

Canada’s outright detention of Meng at the behest of the United States has shocked Chinese society and also struck the global business community. Global stock markets fell the day the news was announced; analysts generally believe the drop was caused by Meng’s detention, which shows the very negative signal that the U.S.–Canada action sent globally.

That Canada police are treating Meng so inhumanely — putting handcuffs and leg irons on her before trial or conviction — is particularly hard for the deeply concerned Chinese public to accept. Isn’t Canada a country of the rule of law and respect for human rights? How could they do something that looks like the act of a barbaric country?

In any case Canada has gone too far. In Chinese there is a saying: this is playing the tiger’s accomplice. Meng Wanzhou did not break Canadian law. Even if the U.S. accuses her of violating U.S. law, whether the U.S. evidence is sufficient and whether the charges hold are all uncertain.

There are reports that Canadian prosecutors allege Meng served as a director of a subsidiary that later split from Huawei and that the company violated U.S. sanctions on Iran by selling some computer equipment to Iran. Whether the facts are as the Canadian prosecutors claim is highly disputed. Even if, hypothetically, that so-called evidence could be sustained in the U.S., there remains substantial judicial room for debate about the legal nature of that situation.

So far, in most cases where foreign companies’ behavior was found to violate U.S. sanctions on Iran, the main responses have been fines and sanctions. There are many global companies that have been sanctioned by the U.S.; it is not one or two. Many European companies have also been involved. The EU currently still encourages European firms not to withdraw from Iran. Should the executives of those companies who travel or transit in Canada all be arrested and thrown into detention and be handcuffed and shackled?

Meng Wanzhou was only ever a director of the Hong Kong company called “Skycom,” which the U.S. says violated the ban; why did the U.S. ask Canada specifically to arrest her, while other people from that company were not targeted? Shouldn’t Canada use its head?

Canada is a sovereign and independent country. Although Canada–U.S. relations are special, Canada should be neutral in treating Meng and should not blindly follow the United States. While providing judicial assistance to the U.S., it should respect the basic spirit of the law and firmly refuse any influence that long-standing U.S. prejudice against Huawei and Huawei’s founder Ren Zhengfei might have on this case.

If Canada treats Meng unjustly to express its loyalty to the United States, that will not be in Canada’s national interest. If Canada extradites Meng to the U.S., and even denies her bail, the goodwill it would win from the U.S. will be limited. But Ottawa’s doing so is absolutely unacceptable to Chinese society. Many members of the Chinese public will write a heavy ledger against Canada; they will certainly demand that the Chinese government severely punish Canada. China–Canada relations face the risk of a serious retrogression, which is also an injury to the interests of the Canadian public.

We hope the Canadian side will handle this matter seriously and properly, treat Meng humanely, allow her bail, and let the matter quickly move toward fully restoring Meng Wanzhou’s freedom. Chinese society has always had much respect for Canada. We hope the way Canada handles this matter will ultimately prove that it is indeed the kind of country that has earned Chinese people’s good impressions.

Editorial: Why, aside from resolutely fighting back, China has no choice

According to the US side, on July 6 Washington will impose tariffs on the first-batch list of Chinese goods worth $34 billion. That will inevitably immediately trigger equal retaliation from China, and it also means the real start of a US‑China trade war. This will undoubtedly have huge shocks for China and the United States as well as for global trade.

In the coming two weeks, is there still a chance to avoid this trade war?

Washington’s “extortion to the limit” has aroused broad indignation in Chinese society, but there are indeed some who think perhaps we could give ground a little, take a loss in order to get the other side to return to reason. They are not the mainstream, but they have some influence. One widely circulated argument is that the US economy is very strong, and China may not be able to win a head‑on fight; hard fighting might even affect China’s strategic opportunity window.

We must say this view is too naive and unrealistic. For China today, apart from resolutely fighting back, there is no other choice.

First, Washington has pushed China into a corner; there is nowhere left to retreat. China “doesn’t want a trade war,” and to that end has made its maximum efforts. In the previous rounds of consultations, the Chinese side has acted with great sincerity and flexibility, trying as much as possible to reach consensus with the US and find concrete ways to resolve differences. But perhaps this made some in the US mistakenly think that “China is afraid,” and they repeatedly tore up agreements, not taking China’s latter‑half statement—“not afraid to fight”—seriously.

One simple example: food security is the country’s foundation. As a nation of 1.4 billion people, China has always insisted on self‑sufficiency in staple grains and accordingly has subsidized staple grain production — a practice that is almost universal globally. For example, if international rice price is 3,000 yuan/ton, China’s government purchase price is 3,900 yuan/ton; if international cotton price is 14,000 yuan/ton, China’s purchase price is 19,000 yuan/ton. The US strongly demands that China “reduce or even eliminate agricultural subsidies” and expand imports of US agricultural products. Imagine, if China cancelled or reduced these subsidies, how many farmers would be bankrupted? And how much would our food security depend on the US, and how great would the risk be? The US said it would stop selling chips to ZTE, putting a giant enterprise on the brink of destruction. If one day the US said it would not sell food to China and Chinese people ended up with no rice to eat, that would be equivalent to the US strangling China’s throat.

The Trump administration’s appetite is getting larger and larger. If China yields on core principles and interests in the face of crude “trade extortion,” it will not win Washington’s respect or restraint; instead it will spur the US to press its advantage further on trade, and perhaps in future even try to play the Taiwan card to coerce China. The appetite of a tyrant is insatiable: after taking a city for a night’s sleep, he eyes the neighboring lands, and “Qin’s soldiers come again.” For now, the only way is to fight back resolutely, and draw a clear “trade ninety‑third line” to stop US greed.

Second, in facing the US’s current trade cudgel, there is no precedent of a victim country “surrendering”; not even Japan accepted humiliation. Belgian Prime Minister Michel and French President Macron both described Washington’s approach as “holding a gun to the EU’s head,” and in that situation the EU “would not negotiate anything.” In world trade history, responses to trade protectionism have always been “tit for tat”; only by reciprocity can one deter further adventures by “trade predators.”

True, the US has the world’s largest GDP and more ammunition for a trade fight. But do not forget: the countries and organizations that are now standing up to the US have a combined GDP of more than $40 trillion, more than twice the US’s nearly $20 trillion GDP, and their available resources are correspondingly much larger. If the US truly starts a global trade war, being the unjust party it would surely lose.

If the trade war kicks off in July, at least $75 billion worth of US products will be affected — including about $40 billion of items that Canada, the EU, Mexico and others have proposed as retaliatory tariff lists against the steel and aluminum tariffs, and $34 billion of products subject to China’s retaliatory tariffs. A study commissioned by the National Retail Federation and the Consumer Technology Association shows that the US would lose at least 134,000 jobs a year because of a trade war. These are also pains the US will find hard to bear.

Third, the worst outcome of fighting back is still better than the consequences of surrender. Trade experts interviewed by the Global Times conducted assessments and concluded that although China would suffer losses, it can withstand them. At worst, if the US put into effect the threatened $250 billion — $50 billion of products taxed at 25% and $200 billion of products taxed at 10% — that would amount to $30 billion a year, about 5% of total Sino‑US trade. Taking into account all distributed risks, US actions might shave 0.1 percentage point off China’s economic growth. Compared with the great storms New China has already weathered in its history, this loss is not extremely severe. The key is that our morale must be strong and that we must have a full set of policy reserves.

At least in theory, the imminent trade war could still be avoided if Washington comes to its senses and reins itself in. Otherwise, it should prepare for a heavy blow from China.

response.english_translation:
Editorial: The "Afghanistan effect" will play out around the world in many versions

U.S. Vice President Harris on Tuesday fiercely attacked China for "coercion" and "intimidation" in the South China Sea region in Singapore, and claimed the United States "stands with our allies and partners."

Harris is eager to use a tough posture toward China and verbal commitments to offset the credibility crisis caused by America's ignominious retreat from Afghanistan, and to urge a few Southeast Asian countries to confront China. But the chaotic images of the U.S. withdrawal at Kabul airport speak louder than a thousand words; countries in Southeast Asia hardened by geopolitics see this all too clearly.

Even before this latest upheaval in Afghanistan, normal countries — including most U.S. allies — refused to take sides between China and the United States. The Biden administration has spent more than half a year trying everything possible to build an anti-China united front, but much of its成果 has been superficial. No savvy Southeast Asian country has shown willingness to lead a confrontation with China. America's coercion and inducements in the region are increasingly showing signs of failure.

The U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan and the contraction of its military presence in the Middle East, combined with a pivot to intensify geostrategic competition with China in Southeast Asia, will soon be proven ineffective. This strategy cannot make Singapore, Vietnam and others take risks for U.S. interests against China, and the decline of U.S. influence in the Middle East will create serious uncertainties that could threaten American interests — for which the United States will surely pay.

The only countries the U.S. can probably still deceive are small states like Lithuania. Lithuania has led the way in developing relations with Taiwan in a manner that undermines the One-China principle, trading on absolute U.S. protection. But Lithuania has clearly misjudged the situation: it is now confronting two major powers, China and Russia, at the same time. China and Russia, including together with Belarus, will have many means to impose long-term sanctions and strikes against it, making it pay a heavy price.

The Taiwan authorities cling tightly to the U.S. but Washington cannot give them unlimited support and "go to the ends of the earth" for them. The fundamental nature of U.S.-Taiwan ties — that the U.S. wants to use Taiwan to harass and contain the mainland — will not change. When faced with the mainland's real determination to settle matters militarily, America's retreat is inevitable; the Democratic Progressive Party authorities are pursuing a strategically sleepwalking course.

China and Russia should join forces and other capabilities so that the United States is embarrassed over Lithuania and Taiwan, producing an "Afghanistan effect" that may take different forms but that the world can understand. America's hand has reached too far; China and Russia should cut off its arm at some of Washington's points of arrogant showmanship.

The "Afghanistan effect" in Southeast Asia is already quietly playing out. Compared with a few years ago, Singapore's clearly pro-U.S. posture has become more neutral, and Vietnam is distinguishing the South China Sea issue from its overall China-Vietnam relationship. These are Southeast Asian countries prudently anticipating the "Afghanistan effect" in advance; Vietnam, in particular, has deep "Saigon memories."

The United States has just over 300 million people and its industrial production is far below its peak. It thinks it can bully a country like China — four times its population, rapidly developing, diligent and innovative — simply because of its super military power, financial hegemony, and a few key technologies. China will prove to it with facts that it is mistaken.

America's mistake is that its ambition has swollen; it seriously overestimates its appeal and the geopolitical significance of so-called "shared values" with some countries, and misjudges what China's rise means for countries that feel uncomfortable. Washington believes its hegemony is truly existential for many countries, and that other states will equate defending U.S. hegemony with their own core interests and be willing to pay any price.

Because its lines are stretched too thin, the "Afghanistan scenarios" for the U.S. will be replayed in various forms across the globe; this will be a process of gradually damaging America's influence and reputation. It will also be a vivid portrayal of America's decline.

response.english_translation:
Editorial: Intimidating China — Europe’s anti-China forces will hit a brick wall

After China announced countermeasures against EU sanctions on China and placed 10 EU individuals and 4 organizations on our sanctions list, some in Europe reacted strongly, calling China’s counter-sanctions "unacceptable." The European Parliament on Tuesday even cancelled a meeting to discuss the EU-China Investment Agreement, and some European lawmakers threatened to make China’s delisting from sanctions a condition for advancing the agreement. Voices advocating “punishing China” by blocking the agreement have been amplified by certain anti-China forces.

We must tell those forces that the EU-China Investment Agreement is a product of mutual reciprocity, not a gift from Europe to China. If the European Parliament wants to block that agreement and use it as a bargaining chip against China, let them take that up with European countries; if all those countries agree, then let’s pretend last year’s negotiations between China and the EU never happened. But they must not use this matter to threaten China — we despise that attitude.

China is already the EU’s largest trading partner. Look at how many German cars run on Chinese streets, how many French and Italian fashion items Chinese women use, and how many Chinese travel to Europe in a normal year. With China’s good development momentum in the coming years, what right do shallow European parliamentarians have to threaten us by refusing to approve the Investment Agreement? We have not yet used shelving the advancement of that agreement to send a warning to Brussels!

Chinese society has always respected Europe; we have never taken the initiative to pick fights with EU countries on any matter. It has been some anti-China European politicians and certain official bodies dominated by them who provoked us, turning their arrogance and prejudice toward China into action and harming China’s interests. We have every reason to respond.

This time the EU fired the first shot of sanctions against China for the first time in over 30 years — did they expect Beijing to swallow it? Or did they expect that, before China retaliated, Beijing would have to seek their permission? Who granted them the right to be so willful and untouchable?

Even after the mutual sanctions, we still value our relationship with the EU and are willing to return to normal exchanges. But the first principle of normal exchanges is equality and mutual respect. China has its core interests and bottom lines; restoring peace, stability and prosperity in Xinjiang is among the central elements of that principle. The EU should not lightly step on China’s toes; if it continues to do so, China’s response will not be polite.

There are no major conflicts of interest between China and the EU; the two sides ought to be partners in development. It is hard for many Chinese to understand why some European forces insist on creating confrontation between China and Europe. Let the bullets of friction fly a bit. We hope this produces a special effect of increasing mutual understanding; short-term frictions could objectively be helpful for long-term mutual recognition and cooperation. We also hope the EU as a whole acts rationally; if the EU goes astray on its China policy, we can only go along and give them due company.

In other words, China is both an active advocate of China-EU cooperation and a calm accepter of any conflict between the two sides. How China-EU relations develop does not depend solely on words and talks; both sides must shape it through complex interactions. We have good initiatives, but we also know you cannot force a fruit to ripen. China’s future development depends primarily on internal drivers; for us, doing our own work well, including governing Xinjiang, is the top priority.

Some European elites assume that because Sino-US relations are strained, China needs Europe more, and thus they have grown strategically arrogant. That is a shallow view.

A more independent EU also needs China. American power is relatively weakening, but the US is trying to preserve an "America First" order by bullying, constantly instrumentalizing European countries. In promoting a multipolar world, China-EU cooperation benefits both sides, but there is no condition under which Europe can blackmail China.

Editorial: If the US and Taiwan dare to “rename,” they will certainly make them pay a heavy price

According to the Financial Times of the UK, Washington is seriously considering Taiwan’s request to change the name of its representative office in Washington from the “Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office” to the “Taiwan Representative Office.” The report says White House Indo-Pacific Coordinator Kurt Campbell supports the renaming and that the U.S. side is assessing the risks of doing so. This report has provoked a strong reaction on the island; both U.S. and Taiwan officials have refused to respond directly.

Other reports say senior U.S. and Taiwan “national security” officials held a face-to-face meeting in Annapolis, Maryland, less than an hour’s drive from Washington. These two items of news came out shortly after the phone call between the Chinese and U.S. heads of state.

It must be pointed out that if the U.S. and Taiwan carry out the above name change, it would mean Washington has essentially abandoned the One-China policy and would constitute a major incident surrounding the Taiwan issue. Lithuania previously announced it would use the name “Taiwan” to set up representative offices with Taiwan and suffered a fierce Chinese boycott. If the United States does the same, there is no doubt it will have a broad demonstrative effect among its allies and bring about a wave of renamings of Taiwanese representative offices in the capitals of those countries.

The U.S. side clearly knows this matter is not trivial; they are now in a phase of floating the idea and testing the mainland’s reaction.

What’s there to test? If they push things to the brink of a showdown, the mainland has no choice but to welcome the challenge and prepare to confront them.

If the U.S. switches to using the name “Taiwan Representative Office” for Taiwan’s mission in the U.S., the mainland’s diplomatic reaction will not be less than our reaction to Lithuania. In that case it is fully to be expected that China would recall its ambassador from the U.S., and that could well be the mainland’s “minimum response” diplomatically; otherwise China would have no way to assert the One-China principle.

At present, under U.S. instigation and encouragement, some Western countries are itching to play the “Taiwan card.” If China responds by suppressing small provocations and enlarging them, that will not work. If we are to uphold the One-China bottom line, we must stop the U.S.; otherwise it would mean we are prepared to accept more “Taiwan representative offices” appearing in the capitals of a number of countries.

Diplomatic means clearly are not enough. If the U.S. and Taiwan go ahead with the renaming, they will already be touching the red line of the Anti-Secession Law; the mainland needs to employ severe economic and military measures to strike at the arrogance of the U.S. and Taiwan. At that time the mainland should impose harsh economic sanctions on Taiwan, up to and including, depending on circumstances, an economic blockade of Taiwan.

Militarily, in that situation the mainland’s warplanes should fly over Taiwan island and bring Taiwan’s airspace into the People’s Liberation Army’s patrol range — this is a step the mainland must sooner or later take, and the renaming of U.S.-Taiwan representative offices would provide ample justification for the mainland to strengthen its assertion of sovereignty over Taiwan in this way. We expect Taiwan’s military will not dare to stop PLA aircraft flying over the island; if Taiwan’s forces dare to open fire, then we will resolutely deliver a decisive and devastating strike against the “Taiwan independence” forces.

The important point is that if the mainland tolerates the U.S. and Taiwan this time, they will certainly go further next. It is said that at the Annapolis meeting the Taiwan participants included “Foreign Minister” Joseph Wu. If that is true, next time they will hold the meeting publicly, perhaps even in the U.S. State Department building. And there is the so-called “Summit for Democracy” at the end of the year — if we don’t curb U.S.-Taiwan momentum, Washington might actually invite Tsai Ing-wen to attend, which would be even worse in nature than Lee Teng-hui’s 1995 visit to the U.S. under the pretext of being an alumnus.

If China swallows all this for the sake of peace, will peace come? If we do not hit back decisively and forcefully, U.S. warships will dock in Taiwan, fighter jets will land in Taiwan, and its troops may even be stationed in Taiwan — in that case where will China’s great-power prestige be placed? How would China maintain the system for defending its own interests internationally?

The fact is that a contest of wills has already formed around the Taiwan issue. Since Beijing has declared Taiwan to be China’s core interest, we will certainly protect this bottom line of national interest with resolute action, no matter what the cost. If the DPP authorities truly dare to risk provoking a war by pushing the renaming, and if the U.S., fresh from defeat in Afghanistan, is not afraid of being dragged into a new war, what is there for the mainland to fear?

It seems the Taiwan Strait will sooner or later see a violent storm — one that will truly shake the earth. Given current U.S.-Taiwan trends, if they pull back this step now, they will take another step forward next time; we must be fully prepared now, ready at any moment to “break their legs” in the Taiwan Strait.

The United States has been playing word games, hoping to avoid competition with China turning into open conflict; we must tell them with actions that on the Taiwan issue competition with China will inevitably become a serious conflict, with no room for maneuver.
